subject: Ag producers feeling squeezed by diesel despite executive action
posts:
Squeezed by soaring fuel costs, farmers and truckers face empty relief as executive diesel waivers fall flat.
Evidence: Global shocks, empty waivers, continued squeeze
#Aletheia #Montana #Ag 🌐

The administration claimed executive orders permitting red-dyed diesel and foreign imports would blunt fuel cost spikes for agricultural producers and truckers.
Stated Judgement: (+0.8, 0.0) — Good Preference

Economists and agricultural leaders confirm local diesel prices remain near historic highs driven by global conflicts, rendering temporary exemptions and logistical hurdles useless.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.9, -0.8) — Lesser Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception.
Executive photo-ops mask global energy realities, offering illusory waivers while farmers shoulder punishing fuel surcharges.
Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 12.5, z: 2)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Executive Waivers: FAIL (-0.8, -0.7) — Too late and logistically impractical.
- Import Pledges: FAIL (-0.9, -0.8) — Fails to shift global pricing baselines.
As conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine spikes global diesel prices, Montana officials issued temporary dyed-diesel exemptions and federal import pledges to blunt costs ahead of midterms.

The Poison:
Using headline-grabbing executive orders as political theater while actual agricultural supply chains and profit margins bleed from unaddressed global fuel spikes.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing political signalling (WHO/WHAT) with systemic economic reality. Blaming local rules while global oil markets and refinery strikes dictate high prices.

Social Physics Analysis:
Actors execute a Smart Selfish Maneuver, packaging cosmetic pretexts and delayed waivers as solutions to project competence while avoiding systemic economic truths.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Deception. (ψ=-0.8, u=-0.9)

The Unavoidable Truth: Cosmetic fuel waivers cannot override global commodity markets or save farmers from delayed relief.

The Unavoidable Lie: Executive decrees instantly solve structural energy shocks.

Alethekanon:
Political optics substitute for actual economic intervention, leaving producers to absorb unmitigated fuel surcharges under hollow pretexts.

Awwthekanon:
Our hard-working ranchers and truck drivers feed the nation while carrying the crushing weight of global crises and empty political promises.

Brothekanon:
Classic political magic trick—slapping a flashy headline on a fuel waiver that arrives too late to help anyone actually harvesting grain.

Spirithekanon:
"He who oppresses the poor to increase his wealth gives to the rich and will only come to poverty." Proverbs 22:16 PASS
Shifting political theater onto struggling producers while offering empty relief is a moral failure.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Ag producers feeling squeezed by diesel despite executive action

Industry groups and economists are skeptical that new imports and dyed-fuel waivers will move the needle on spiking diesel prices.

Actual Article Body:
Montana Free Press

Montana's independent nonprofit news source.

Tim Brunner, a rancher near Great Falls who serves as president of the Montana Cattlemen’s Association, said he doesn’t expect recent efforts by President Donald Trump and Gov. Greg Gianforte to mitigate the high cost of diesel to result in much financial relief for his ranch.

Lt. Gov. Kristen Juras issued an executive order on Friday that allows commercial vehicles engaged “directly in agricultural or timber industry operations” to use red-dyed diesel on public roads until Nov. 23. The order comes about a week after President Donald Trump signed an executive order suspending a federal law that bans the use of red-dyed diesel in vehicles on public roads.

Red-dyed diesel is the same as diesel — a fuel commonly used in heavy machinery, semi trucks and many pickups — except for its color and substantially lower tax rate. The dyed fuel is reserved mostly for agricultural use in Montana. That’s why it’s exempt from taxes that pay for highways, and why it’s usually illegal to drive with red-dyed diesel on public roads.

On Friday, Trump announced on Truth Social a plan to import about 800,000 tons of diesel fuel — about a day and a half’s worth of U.S. demand — from Russia before the end of November. The post also indicated that another 4 million tons will arrive from Russia sometime later.

The price of diesel has spiked this year as a result of the U.S. conflict with Iran and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, prompting federal and state government efforts to mitigate the price spikes ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Near-record diesel prices are putting pressure on Montana farmers who depend on fuel to run combines, tractors and other equipment, and also increasing the cost of transporting goods once they leave the farm.

Jeffrey Michael, director of the University of Montana’s Bureau of Business and Economic Research, is also skeptical that the Trump-announced diesel imports will ease prices. Diesel fuel is priced similarly — currently at a historic high because of the foreign conflicts — worldwide. Newly available domestic supplies in the U.S. probably won’t bring down the global price.

Montana ranks No. 4 among American states for diesel vehicles per capita, according to Michael. And it’s No. 8 in the amount spent on diesel per dollar of gross domestic product, an economic measure that totals the state’s output of goods and services.

Walt Schweitzer, president of the Montana Farmers Union and a frequent critic of Trump’s trade policies, also expressed doubt that new diesel imports will help agricultural producers.

“If he really wanted to have a positive impact on our diesel price, he would quit exporting our diesel and keep it here,” Schweitzer said.

Schweitzer also highlighted logistical obstacles that might undermine Gianforte’s efforts to provide financial relief to truckers. For instance, gas station aisles with dyed-diesel pumps — there is often one per station — may not physically accommodate semi trucks. Plus, increased demand for dyed diesel may also increase the chances of exhausting rural supply chains. And because the legality of driving on public roads with dyed diesel varies by state, Schweitzer said, the new policy may be “confusing and difficult to manage” for interstate truckers.

And for Montana farmers, he said the policy comes “too late.”

“Most of the farmers that are hauling grain to the elevators have done that already,” Schweitzer said.

Brunner, the Great Falls rancher, is also skeptical that the state’s temporary allowance for dyed diesel will provide much relief. He pointed out that the dye stays in vehicle tanks even after the fuel is spent, so if a driver gets pulled over after the exemption expires in late November, a test could show a false positive and lead to fines.

“In another year, get your tank dipped. It shows red. There’s $1,000 right there,” Brunner said.

Brunner is trying to keep his ranch’s books balanced. Over the weekend, he hired a few semi trucks and drivers to bring his herd, which summers 125 miles to the north, back home. He got his bill on Monday. Unlike the one in spring, it included an 8.5% diesel surcharge.

“It’s ridiculous,” Brunner said.

And he has even more diesel-related costs on the horizon. When he ships cattle to feedlots in the Midwest in the coming months, he’ll pay for the fuel premium. It will also show up when he sells and ships his hay.

“What doesn’t diesel affect?” Brunner asked. “Every single thing we do, everything we eat and use, everything depends on diesel.”
